He's wrong to say "technically yes". There's absolutely no way the Apollo 11 retroreflector -- let alone the much larger and more fragile 14 and 15 retroreflectors -- could have been deposited on the moon with 20th century technology. Getting those down in one piece robotically would be slightly more difficult than landing the Mars rovers was.

Also they're not crystals per se or a silvered mirror like the one in your bathroom. They're more like a honeycomb of shiny earth metal crystals, which is why they're so fragile. You could literally tear one apart with your bare hands.

There's absolutely no way the Apollo 11 retroreflector -- let alone the much larger and more fragile 14 and 15 retroreflectors -- could have been deposited on the moon with 20th century technology

Impossible to set up this robotically, but we could send humans back and forth?

Yes, exactly. If they'd been trying to land something that fragile in a much larger lander, that would have been (relatively) simple. The Soviets did exactly that in '70 and '75, when they landed Lunokhod 1 and 2, respectively, which were roughly six cubic feet each and weighed about 1,800 lbs. Much of their size and weight was essentially packing material to keep their sensors and tools (including their top-mounted retroreflectors) in one piece during the extremely rough lunar landing. In fact Lunokhod 2's mirror was badly damaged in the landing and only retained about 1/5th of its reflectivity. It's only with modern microcomputers and miniaturization that it became possible for a probe to land itself without basically just crashing and being built hard enough to survive it.

A retroreflector could have been left on the surface by any of the successful sample probe missions (Soviet missions Luna 16, 20 and 24; NASA never managed to a probe lander back), but any such reflector would have been buried in lunar soil and rendered useless when it took off. The entire purpose of running a manned mission was to deliver experiments that couldn't survive a landing like Surveyor 3's, which literally bounced 35 feet off the moon (and again 11 feet) before it came to rest. This was a soft landing by 60s robotics standards, practically ideal for a craft that size. A much larger lander (and therefore one with greater inertia) gave the crude analog robotics of the time a much wider margin of error and time to correct, which is how the Soviets got two rovers the size of sedans down in (more or less) one piece.

I suppose it's theoretically possible NASA landed a car or two of their own on the moon for the express purpose of placing a relatively small retroreflector there and just didn't tell anybody, but they'd had to have hidden the launch itself somehow. Rocket launches tend to attract attention. If you think NASA has been hiding silent, invisible rockets since the 60s, there's not much I can say to disabuse you of any notion of what they did or didn't launch to space or land on the moon.

Sure, it's used whenever someone makes a curve - even if they don't know it. It's there.

It's defined as a "fixed line used in describing a curve or a surface."

If you have a parabola, it's the given line that's not through the focus, but is equidistant to the focus. Engineers use it in the design of things like suspension bridges, ski lifts, gondolas, and stuff like that - it points to where (in those cases) the high point of gravitation would be (even though said spot isn't technically in the parabola itself). It points to where the center of gravity (or most gravitational force) would be.

There's other things where it gets used, I guess doing parabolic orbital mechanics uses it a bit.
